messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rafael Hernandez had always been drawn to the creative precision of architecture. As a successful architect in his late forties, he took pride in designing spaces that felt both functional and beautiful. But it was on one fateful evening, while working late at his office, that Rafael's life took an abrupt turn. He witnessed a violent altercation between two strangers outside his building, an event that would forever sear itself into his memory. As the days passed, Rafael found himself increasingly on edge. The sound of raised voices or the scent of cigarette smoke – reminiscent of that night – could send him spiraling back to the traumatic scene. He'd feel a familiar wave of nausea wash over him, and before he knew it, he was reliving the event as if it were happening all over again. His memories of that night remained stubbornly disjointed, refusing to cohere into a linear narrative. When attempting to recount the events to his wife or colleagues, Rafael would struggle to find the words, as if the language itself had been torn from him. As time went on, these triggers began to exert an insidious influence over Rafael's daily life. Upon entering any room or building, he'd instinctively scan for exits, a habit that left him feeling jumpy and easily startled. He couldn't shake the sense of being exposed unless his back was against a wall where he could see the entire space unfold before him. This hyper-vigilance had become second nature to Rafael; it was as if his mind had become wired to constantly scan for threats. These intrusive thoughts also led Rafael down a dark path of self-blame and negative appraisals. He'd convinced himself that there must be something fundamentally flawed within him, some intrinsic fault that made him a magnet for such horrors. This gnawing sense of helplessness had isolated him from those around him – friends, family, even his wife. They couldn't possibly understand what he was going through; Rafael felt like an outsider looking in on his own life. As the weeks turned into months, Rafael's avoidance behaviors began to take a toll on his relationships and work. His wife, Maria, grew increasingly concerned about his withdrawal from social events and family gatherings. At the office, Rafael found himself struggling to concentrate, his designs marred by mistakes and missteps. It was as if the traumatic event had awakened a persistent threat response within him – always lurking just beneath the surface, waiting to pounce. One day, while working on a new project, Rafael's anxiety spiked when he caught a whiff of cigarette smoke wafting from outside his office window. The scent instantly transported him back to that fateful night, and with it came the familiar wave of nausea and disorientation. His mind racing, Rafael quickly excused himself, citing a sudden case of food poisoning as an excuse for his abrupt departure. In truth, Rafael knew he couldn't outrun these triggers forever. He was exhausted from living in this constant state of high alert, trapped within a self-reinforcing cycle of threat and fear. As the days went by, Rafael began to realize that he needed help – not just to manage his symptoms but to break free from the crushing weight of his own negative appraisals. As he sat in his dimly lit office, staring blankly at the computer screen, Rafael finally made the decision to seek professional help. He knew it wouldn't be easy, but he couldn't shake the feeling that there had to be more to life than this suffocating fog of anxiety and fear. For the first time in months, a glimmer of hope flickered within him – perhaps with guidance, Rafael could learn to tame his inner demons and find a way back to the person he once was.
